full_judgment:
5. The learned Munsif having considered the oral and documentary evidence and also by reference to the C.S. Khatian exht. 5 held that the suit premises which appertained to distinct plots namely 1253, 1354 and 1255 of Khatian No. 803 did not appertain to Joypurhat Hat which comprised of plots Nos. 1238 and 1239 and as such they were retainable lands of the plaintiffs and that Govt. was not entitled to acquire the same nor did it stand acquired under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. With the aforesaid finding the learned Munsif decreed the suit by his judgment dated 28.7.72. 

 10. The plaintiffs have clearly asserted in the plaint that the suit premises appertain to plot Nos. 1253, 1254 and 1255 of C.S. Khatian No. 803 and also asserted that Joypurhat Hat appertains to different and distinct plots namely plot Nos.1238 and 1239.in the written statement the defendants did not deny this fact at all. On the other hand the defendants' document namely Exht. 'D' which is an order of S.D.O. also clearly mentions that the Joypurhat Hat appertains to plot No. 1238. In that order all that has been said is that one of the plaintiffs has encroached upon a part of plot No. 1238. Thus it is absolutely clear that the Joypurhat Hat comprised of two distinct plots namely C.S. Plot Nos. 1238 and 1239 whereas the pre-sent suit lands are comprised of different plot Nos. 1253, 1254 and 1255. So there is absolutely no scope to hold that the suit premises are within Joypurhat Hat. Exht. 11 the C.S. Map does not at all show and cannot at all show that the suit premises comprised of C.S. plot Nos. 1253 and 1255 arc within Joypurhat Hat which is comprised of quite different C.S. Plot Nos. 1238 and 1239. Thus it is found that the learned Additional District Judge misread the document Exht. 11 and Exht. D in coming to his finding that the suit premises were covered by the Joypurhat Hat. On the contrary the C.S. Khatian Exht. 5 clearly show that the suit premises were outside the Joypurhat Hat though it was to the contiguous south of the said Hat. For the aforesaid reasons I find that the learned Munsif rightly found that the suit premises being outside the Joypurhat Hat were retainable land of the plaintiffs and that the same could not be acquired and also could not stand acquired under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and also that the plaintiffs' title holds good in respect of the suit premises and they were entitled to retain their possession. The learned Additional District Judge committed an error of law in coming to a contrary finding without any kind of basis for the same. 

 12. P.O. 90/72 actually came into force on 3rd August, 1972 and it provides that only those suits, appeals, and proceedings which are pending or which are deemed to be pending on the date of commencement of P.O. 90/72 that is on 3rd August, 1972 shall abate. But as I have already noted this suit was disposed of on 28-7-72 and by no stretch of imagination it could be deemed to be pending on 3-8-72 that is on the commencement of P.O. 90/72 when neither the suit nor the present appeal was pending in fact the present appeal was preferred on 25-2-74 that is long two years after and this appeal was preferred not by the plain, tiffs to challenge the acquisition but by the defendant to support the acquisition and P.O. 90/72 was not applicable even to this appeal. In the aforesaid circumstances, the learned Additional District Judge committed an error of law in holding that the suit was liable to abate under P.O. 90/72.
